<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wild|6924|wildcat}}</noinclude>esome; giddy; light-hearted.

{{smaller block|Pardon me if I suspect you still; you are too ''wild'' and airy to be constant to that affection.
{{right|''Shirley'', Witty Fair One, ii. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|That the ''wild'' little thing should take wing, and fly away the Lord knows whither! {{right|''Colman'', Jealous Wife, iii.}}}}

<poem>A ''wild'', unworldly-minded youth, given up
To his own eager thoughts.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Wordsworth'', Prelude, iv.}}}}

{{smaller block|Philip was a dear, good, frank, amiable, ''wild'' fellow, and they all loved him. {{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, v.}}}}

'''2.''' Boisterous; tempestuous; stormy; violent; turbulent; furious; uncontrolled: used in both a physical and a moral sense.

<poem>But that still use of grief makes ''wild'' grief tame,
My tongue should to thy ears not name my boys
Till that my nails were anchor’d in thine eyes.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4. 229.}}}}

<poem>His passions and his virtues lie confused,
And mixt together in so ''wild'' a tumult
That the whole man is quite disfigured in him.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Addison'', Cato, iii. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|Long after night had overclouded the prospect I heard a ''wild'' wind rushing among trees.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, v.}}}}

'''3†.''' Bold; brave; daring; wight.

<poem>Of the gretist of Grece & of gret Troy,
That he hade comyng with in company, & knew well the persons,
As the worthiest to wale & ''wildest'' in Armys.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4023.}}}}

'''4.''' Loose and disorderly in conduct; given to going beyond bounds in pleasurable indulgence; ungoverned; more or less dissolute, wayward, or unrestrained in conduct; prodigal.

{{smaller block|He kept company with the ''wild'' prince and Poins.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 2. 74.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Suppose he has beene ''wild'', let me assure you
He ’s now reclaim’d, and has my good opinion.</poem>
{{right|''Brome'', Sparagus Garden, iv. 7.}}}}
'''5.''' Reckless; rash; ill-considered; extravagant; out of accord with reason or prudence; haphazard: as, a ''wild'' venture; ''wild'' trading.
{{smaller block|<poem>If I chance to talk a little ''wild'', forgive me;
I had it from my father. ''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., i. 4. 26.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|Are not our streets daily filled with ''wild'' pieces of justice and random penalties?
{{right|''Addison'', Tatler, No. 253.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''wildest'' opinions of every kind were abroad, “divers and strange doctrines,” with every wind of which men, having no longer an anchor whereby to hold, were carried about and tossed to and fro.
{{right|''Southey'', Bunyan, p. 16.}}}}
{{smaller block|Johnson, the young bowler, is getting ''wild'', and bowls a ball almost wide to the off.
{{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown’s School-Days, ii. 8.}}}}
'''6.''' Extravagant; fantastic; irregular; disordered; weird; queer.
{{smaller block|''Wild'' in their attire.
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, i. 3. 40.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Oft in her [Reason’s] absence mimic fancy wakes
To imitate her: but, misjoining shapes,
''Wild'' work produces oft. ''Milton'', P. L., v. 112.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>When man to man gave willing faith, and loved
A tale the better that ’twas ''wild'' and strange.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Stella.}}}}
'''7.''' Enthusiastic; eager; keen; especially, very eager with delight, excitement, or the like. [Chiefly colloq.]
{{smaller block|<poem>And there,
All ''wild'' to found an University
For maidens, on the spur she fled.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, i.}}}}

{{smaller block|As for Dolly, he was ''wild'' about . . . the town, and the castle, and the Black Forest.
{{right|''Whyte Melville'', White Rose, I. xxviii.}}}}
'''8.''' Excited; roused; distracted; crazy; betokening or indicating excitement or strong emotion.
{{smaller block|Your looks are pale and ''wild''. ''Shak.'', R. and J., v. 1. 28.
<poem>
I grow ''wild'',
And would not willingly believe the truth
Of my dishonour. ''Ford'', Lover’s Melancholy, iv. 1.
</poem>
The fictions of Oates had driven the nation ''wild''.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi.}}}}
'''9.''' Wide of the mark or direct line, standard, or bounds.
{{smaller block|The catcher . . . must begin by a resolution to try for everything, and to consider no ball beyond his reach, no matter how ''wild''.
{{right|''W. Camp'', St. Nicholas, XVII. 831.}}}}
'''10.''' Living in a state of nature; inhabiting the forest or open field; roving; wandering; not tame; not domesticated; feral or ferine: as, a ''wild'' boar; a ''wild'' ox; a ''wild'' cat; a ''wild'' bee. {{smaller|More particularly—(''a'') Noting those animals which in their relation to man are legally styled ''feræ naturæ'' (which see, under ''feræ''): opposed to ''tame''<sup>1</sup>, 1 (''b'') (1).}}
{{smaller block|There aboute ben many goude Hylles and fayre, and many fayre Woodes, and eke ''wylde'' Beestes.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 127.}}}}
{{smaller block|In the same forrest are many ''wild'' Bores and ''wild'' Stagges.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 35. birds are ''wild'' this morning.}}}}

'''11.''' Savage; uncivilized; ungoverned; unrefined; ferocious; sanguinary: noting persons or practices.

{{smaller block|The ''wildest'' savagery. {{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iv. 3. 48.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Nations yet ''wild'' by Precept to reclaim,
And teach ’em Arms, and Arts, in William’s Name.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', Carmen Seculare (1700), st. 37.}}}}

'''12.''' Growing or produced without culture; produced by unassisted nature, or by wild animals; native; not cultivated: as, ''wild'' parsnip; ''wild'' cherry; ''wild'' honey.

{{smaller block|With ''wild'' wood-leaves and weeds I ha’ strew’d his grave.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, iv. 2. 390.}}}}
{{smaller block|It were good to try what would be the effect, if all the blossoms were pulled from a fruit-tree, or the acorns and chestnut buds, etc., from a ''wild'' tree.
{{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 450.}}}}

'''13.''' Desert; not inhabited; uncultivated.

{{smaller block|And that contre is full of grete foreste, and full ''wylde'' to them of the selue contre. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 32.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>These high ''wild'' hills and rough uneven ways
Draws out our miles, and makes them wearisome.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 3. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The plain was grassy, ''wild'', and bare.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Dying Swan.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A desert; an uninhabited and uncultivated tract or region; a waste.
{{smaller block|<poem>The vasty ''wilds''
Of wide Arabia. ''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 7. 41.</poem>
<poem>One Destiny our Life shall guide;
Nor ''Wild'' nor Deep our common Way divide.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', Henry and Emma.}}}}

{{smaller block|We can now tread the regions of fancy without interruption, and expatiate in fairy ''wilds.'' {{right|''Goldsmith,'' Criticisms.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He would linger long
In lonesome vales, making the ''wild'' his home.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley,'' Alastor.}}}}
'''2.''' ''pl.'' Wild animals; game.
{{smaller block|<poem>In mareis and in mores, in myres and in wateres,
Dompynges dyueden [dived]; “deere God,” ich sayde,
“Wher hadden these ''wilde'' suche witt and at what scole?”</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xiv. 169.}}}}
'''At wild†''', crazy; distracted.
{{smaller block|Trust hym never the more for the bylle that I sent yow by hym, but as a man ''at wylde,'' for every thyng that he told me is not trewe. {{right|''Paston Letters,'' III. 179.}}}}

'''wild-brain''' (wīld′brān), ''n.'' A giddy, volatile, heedless person; a harebrain.
{{smaller block|I must let fly my civil fortunes, turn ''wild-brain,'' lay my wits upo’ th’ tenters, you rascals.
{{right|''Middleton,'' Mad World, i. 1.}}}}

'''wildcat''' (wīld′kat), ''n.'' and ''a.'' '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A cat of the original feral stock from which have descended some varieties of the domestic cat; the European ''Felis catus,'' living in a state of nature, not artificially modified in any way.
